record.paper_title: Open Problems and Conjectures on Rational Systems in Three Dimensions
record.original_question: Assume alpha > 0. For the recurrence z_{n+1} = alpha/(1 + product_{i=0}^k z_{n-i}), for n = 0, 1, ..., does every positive solution have a finite limit?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $k \geq 0$ be a fixed nonnegative integer and let $\alpha > 0$ be a positive real parameter. Consider the difference equation
$$z_{n+1} = \frac{\alpha}{1 + \prod_{i=0}^{k} z_{n-i}}, \qquad n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots,$$
with arbitrary positive initial conditions $z_{-k}, z_{-k+1}, \ldots, z_{0} > 0$. Determine whether every positive solution $\{z_n\}_{n \geq -k}$ of this recurrence converges to a finite limit.
artifact.status_search_result: Web search did not return a definitive resolution of this specific conjecture on convergence of positive solutions for the recurrence $z_{n+1} = \alpha/(1+\prod_{i=0}^k z_{n-i})$ for arbitrary $k$. The parser metadata indicates the conjecture has been confirmed, but no clear independent source verifying a full proof for all $k \geq 0$ and all $\alpha > 0$ was located in the search.

status_evidence.title: Convergence of solutions of a system of recurrence equations
status_evidence.snippet: Studies convergence of positive solutions for higher-order rational difference equations of related form.
status_evidence.claim: Convergence-type results are available for related rational recurrences, but this reference does not directly settle the stated conjecture.
